title: Exporting and Importing
objective: Understand how a function is exported from its own module and imported into another file.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Original Code Forge chapter; not aligned to a specific book chapter. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: As a JavaScript project grows, keeping every function in one file gets unwieldy. A module is just a JS file whose functions and values other files can borrow — you mark what a file makes available with export, and pull it into another file with import.

The pattern looks like export function greet(name) { ... } in one file, and import { greet } from './greetings.js'; in another. Once imported, greet works exactly as if it had been defined right there — you just call greet(...) normally.

Code Forge grades a single file at a time, so it can't literally run an import across two files. The examples below show what the split files would contain; in a real project you'd save these as separate .js files, but the assignment itself defines everything directly in one file.
explanation.rule: export makes a function or value available to other files; import brings it in by name from a specific file.

examples.note: greet is exported, so any file can import it by name.

checks.question: Which statement makes a function available for other files to import?

feedback.correct: Correct — export marks a function or value as available to other files via import.
feedback.incorrect: The export keyword is what makes something importable elsewhere.

assignment.title: Forge Toolkit
assignment.brief: Write square(n) that returns n * n — the kind of small helper you'd normally export from its own module — and log square(6).
requirements: Define square(n) that returns n * n.

requirementChecks.label: Does not use import/export in the graded code

hints: square(n) just needs one line: return n * n.
In a real project you'd export square from its own file and import it elsewhere — here it's defined directly since Code Forge grades one file at a time.
Call console.log(square(6)) to print the result.
